title: Homeschoolers on School Teams
resolution: Resolved: Homeschooled students should be allowed to play on their local public school's sports teams.
summary: Some states let homeschooled students try out for public school teams, some leave it to each district, and some don't allow it. Should every homeschooled student get the chance to play?

background.p: The National Center for Education Statistics estimated that 3.4 percent of students ages 5 to 17 were homeschooled in 2012, and a somewhat lower share in 2019. Parents' most common reasons included concern about the school environment (80 percent), a wish to give moral instruction (75 percent) and dissatisfaction with academic instruction (73 percent).

State rules differ a great deal, and they change often. A 2015 count by the Coalition for Responsible Home Education, which supports access, found about 20 states giving homeschoolers full access to public school sports, about 10 allowing it with district approval or part-time enrollment, and about 20 barring it. Bills of this kind are often called "Tebow bills," after quarterback Tim Tebow, who was homeschooled in Florida and played football for a public high school there. Counts since then vary by source, partly because sources define "access" differently.

Texas shows how the rules can work. A 2021 law let each district choose to open University Interscholastic League (UIL) activities to homeschooled students. A 2025 law reversed the default: districts now allow homeschool participation unless the school board votes to opt out. Homeschooled players must meet the same rules as enrolled students and must show grade-level skills on a nationally recognized test in the first six weeks of the school year.

disputed.q: Can schools hold homeschooled players to the same academic standards?
positions: Supporters say tests, parent reports and portfolios can confirm a homeschooled student is keeping up, as states like Texas require.
Opponents say enrolled players must pass every class each grading period under a teacher's grading, and a parent's report or a once-a-year test isn't the same check.

terms.def: Educating a child at home, usually by a parent, instead of enrolling the child in a public or private school. Each state sets its own rules.
Rules a student must meet to play school sports, such as passing grades, attendance, age limits and living in the school's attendance zone.
The organization in each state that runs high school sports and sets eligibility rules, such as the UIL in Texas.
Whether a district must vote to allow something (opt in) or must vote to refuse it (opt out).

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Homeschooled children are part of the community their local school serves, and they should have the same chance to play.

args.claim: Homeschooling families pay for the schools too.
args.warrant: Public schools are funded mostly by local and state taxes that homeschooling families pay. Shutting their children out of a program those taxes support treats them as outsiders in their own district.
args.evidence: State school-funding formulas; testimony in state legislatures, such as the arguments supporters made for the 2021 Texas bill.
args.response: The negative answers that taxes pay for a whole school system that families are free to use or not; paying for roads doesn't entitle you to one lane.

args.claim: Sports teach lessons every child should get.
args.warrant: Teamwork, discipline, losing well and keeping fit are good for any child. In many towns, especially rural ones, the public school team is the only team there is.
args.evidence: Research on youth sports and health and character; reports on rural areas with no club or league teams.
args.response: The negative replies that homeschool leagues, club teams and community sports exist in many places, so the choice isn't school sports or nothing.

args.claim: Many states already do it without serious trouble.
args.warrant: If the policy caused the harms opponents predict, the states that have allowed it for decades would show them. Their experience is the best test.
args.evidence: State laws and athletic association rules (see the reading list); reports from states that have allowed access for many years.
args.response: The negative argues that "no serious trouble" is hard to measure, and complaints about eligibility and roster spots do come up in those states.

args.claim: Fair rules can answer the fairness worries.
args.warrant: States can require homeschoolers to meet the same age, residency, fee and conduct rules as everyone else, plus proof of academic progress. That keeps the playing field level.
args.evidence: The Texas rules, which require a norm-referenced test in the first six weeks and the same eligibility forms as enrolled students.
args.response: The negative replies that a test once a year is a lighter check than passing every class every six weeks, so the field still isn't level.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: School teams belong to the students who attend the school, and families who choose another path accept its trade-offs.

args.claim: School sports are part of school, not a separate service.
args.warrant: A school team represents a community of students who attend classes together. The rule that players must be enrolled students keeps sports tied to the school's mission.
args.evidence: State activities association rules that require enrolled or full-time students; statements from school administrators, such as those quoted in Education Week's 2013 reporting.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the school serves the whole district's children, and the team still represents that community.

args.claim: Eligibility rules can't be applied the same way.
args.warrant: Enrolled players must pass their classes under teachers who grade them, and they can lose eligibility mid-season. A parent who is also the teacher can't be checked the same way.
args.evidence: State no-pass, no-play rules; the critics' arguments in the Texas House Research Organization analysis of the 2021 bill.
args.response: The affirmative replies that states can require outside tests, portfolios or evaluations to confirm progress.

args.warrant: Teams have a fixed number of places. Each spot that goes to a non-enrolled student is one that an enrolled student, who follows all the school's rules, doesn't get.
args.evidence: Team size limits in popular sports; reports from coaches and parents in states that allow access.
args.response: The affirmative answers that spots go to whoever earns them at tryouts, and a homeschooled student who lives in the district is a local student too.

args.claim: It adds costs that school funding doesn't cover.
args.warrant: Districts usually get state money per enrolled student. A student who joins only for sports adds coaching, travel and insurance costs without bringing that funding.
args.evidence: Testimony from school boards associations, such as the Wyoming School Boards Association in 2026; state funding formulas.
args.response: The affirmative replies that states can count these students for activity funding or charge them the same fees enrolled students pay.

strawmen.strawman: They want all the perks of public school without any of the rules.
strawmen.why: Most supporters accept the same eligibility, conduct and fee rules as enrolled students, and many bills add academic checks.
strawmen.steelman: Homeschooled children live in the district and their families help pay for its schools, so with the same eligibility rules and proof of progress they should get the same chance to try out.

strawmen.why: Opponents argue about enrollment, fair eligibility checks, roster spots and funding, not about families' choices.
strawmen.steelman: A school team belongs to the students who attend the school; eligibility can't be checked the same way for students the school doesn't teach, and roster spots and funding are limited.

weak.arg: Homeschoolers are better students, so of course they should play.
weak.why: It doesn't answer the question of who teams are for, and claims about which group does better are disputed and depend on who is studied.

weak.arg: If you want school sports, just go to school.
weak.why: It skips the real arguments about enrollment, fairness and funding, and families choose homeschooling for many reasons that have nothing to do with sports.

aff: How would a school check a homeschooled player's grades during the season?
Should a homeschooled student also be allowed in the band, the play and the robotics team?
What should happen to an enrolled student who loses a roster spot?
neg: Where should a homeschooled student in a small rural town play, if not on the school team?
Do private school students in your district get any access to public programs?
If a homeschooler meets every eligibility rule, what harm does playing cause?
